title: Closed practices
hook: some Indigenous and initiatory practices belong to their peoples and aren't ours to borrow

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Stoic week, and your line was the porch again. Did the evening questions turn up anything? This week walked from Confucian self-cultivation and the ancestors to modern ways: therapy, recovery, rest, the porch. Today, the week ends at a closed door. Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.

For weeks now, this path has been walking into other people's houses of practice. A Zen hall. A gurdwara. A Quaker meeting. A Sufi circle. Those doors have been open: come and sit, come and eat, come and listen. But a few doors in the world are shut on purpose, and a polite visitor learns to notice them. Not shut out of rudeness, and not because the people inside think less of anyone. Shut because what happens inside belongs to a people, or is given only to those who have been brought in. Today is about those doors, and about what a guest does when one of them is closed.
screen: `MOSTLY OPEN DOORS.` → `A FEW SHUT ON PURPOSE.` → `WHAT DOES A GUEST DO?`

segments.voice: A closed practice is one that a community keeps for its own members, or for people it has initiated. The idea is old. In ancient Greece, the rites of Demeter at Eleusis were kept secret by those who took part. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter, in paraphrase, calls them holy rites that no one may break, pry into, or speak aloud. The hymn is happy to tell the story of Demeter and her lost daughter. It will not tell you what happened inside. Story open, rite closed. Today, the idea is often raised by some Indigenous peoples. Certain ceremonies, songs and sacred objects belong to a particular nation or family, passed down by those who have the right to lead them. Some Indigenous leaders have asked outsiders, plainly, not to copy their ceremonies or sell versions of them. Their reasons are their own to give, and they have given them: these are not techniques. They are relationships, with a land, with ancestors, with a people's history, including the times those practices were banned or mocked. Here is the distinction worth carrying. Learning about a practice is usually welcome: reading what a community has chosen to share, listening to its own people tell it, attending when you're invited. Taking it is something else: performing it without the community, borrowing its sacred words for your own use, selling it. And there's a third thing, which is being invited. That door is opened from the inside, not the outside. A path like this one, which draws from many traditions, has to be honest about where its borrowing stops. Some things are offered. Some are not mine to take.
screen: `KEPT FOR MEMBERS OR THE INITIATED.` · `STORY OPEN, RITE CLOSED.` · `RELATIONSHIPS, NOT TECHNIQUES.` · `LEARN ABOUT, DON'T TAKE.` · then, large: `OPENED FROM THE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about one without taking it. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a practice you've heard of that belongs to a particular people, one you've seen copied, or one you've been curious about. Don't try it. Just hold it with respect, the way you'd stand quietly outside a house where a ceremony is going on. Ask: who has the right to lead this? Where could I hear about it from its own people? If you pray, you can pray for that community. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Closed practices. Rites and ceremonies a community keeps for its own members or its initiated, to be learned about with respect and not taken. Today's word.

Your line: not mine to take. Today, find one thing written or told by a member of a community about its own practice, and read or listen without borrowing any of it. Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Communities with closed practices usually share some of their stories and teachings openly while keeping certain ceremonies for members or the initiated; respectful outsiders learn from what the community chooses to share, and take part only when invited by those with the right to lead.

fork.setup: a weekend workshop online offers to teach you a ceremony from an Indigenous nation, led by someone who isn't from that nation. what does today's lesson suggest?
options: sign up: knowledge should be free.
learn about the ceremony from that nation's own people instead.
try the ceremony at home to see if it works.
fork.reveal: learning about is welcome; taking is something else. some Indigenous leaders have asked outsiders, plainly, not to copy or sell their ceremonies.

trapdoor: what you thought: if something is spiritual, everyone has a right to it.
what it means: some rites belong to a people or to the initiated, and a guest learns about them without taking them.
what a scholar hears: the Homeric Hymn to Demeter tells the story of the goddess openly but says the rites at Eleusis may not be pried into or spoken.

notes: The Homeric Hymn to Demeter is paraphrased (no validator-listed translation). Confirm the line range 476–479 for the passage on the secret rites, and that 'no one may break, pry into, or speak aloud' is a fair paraphrase.

Indigenous closed practices are described in general terms, with no nation, ceremony, date or document named, to avoid unsourced claims. A reviewer may want to name a specific public statement by Indigenous leaders (for example, statements by Lakota leaders on the appropriation of ceremonies) with a source.
The phrase 'including the times those practices were banned or mocked' is a general historical statement; confirm it is acceptable without a citation, or add one.
The hook's 'for weeks now' refers to this path's own Block F (days 1352–1419). The examples (Zen hall, gurdwara, Quaker meeting, Sufi circle) come from earlier days in the block.
Week end (days 1408–1414): the review names the week's themes from the index, since days 1408–1411 were not on disk at writing time.
